How Hindsight Helped My Incident Agent Remember Production Failures

Building a memory-powered incident-response system that stops treating every outage as a brand-new problem.

Built with React, FastAPI, Hindsight, Groq, n8n and SQLite

Production incidents have an annoying habit of repeating themselves.

A service fails because of a database connection problem. Someone investigates it, finds the root cause, fixes it, and moves on. A few weeks later, a very similar failure happens again, and another engineer ends up repeating the same investigation.

The information technically exists somewhere, but finding the right incident, understanding what actually caused it, and identifying the fix that worked can still take valuable time.

I wanted to see what incident response would look like if an agent could actually remember those past failures.

That idea became IncidentPilot AI, a memory-powered incident-response system I built with React, FastAPI, Hindsight, Groq, n8n, and SQLite.

Instead of treating every production incident as a completely new problem, IncidentPilot searches its previous experience first. If a similar incident has already been resolved, that memory becomes context for the next recommendation.

The problem I wanted to solve

Most incident tools are good at storing events. They can record a service name, HTTP status code, endpoint, severity, error message, response time, and timestamp.

But during an outage, I care about something more useful:

  • Have we seen this failure before?
  • What caused it last time?
  • What actually fixed it?
  • Was that fix confirmed?
  • Can that experience help me now?

A normal database can store an incident record, but I wanted the agent to reuse the meaning of a previous incident even when the next error was described differently.

That is where persistent agent memory became useful.

How IncidentPilot hangs together

IncidentPilot has a fairly small architecture.

The frontend is built with React and Vite. An engineer can submit an incident containing the affected service, endpoint, status code, error, response time, and severity. That request goes to a FastAPI backend.

From there, the system:

  1. stores the operational incident,
  2. asks Hindsight for similar resolved incidents,
  3. sends the current incident plus the recalled memories to the LLM,
  4. returns a concise recommendation,
  5. lets an engineer confirm the real root cause and successful fix,
  6. stores that confirmed outcome back into Hindsight.

I also built an n8n intake workflow, so an incident can enter through a webhook rather than only through the React form.

The distinction that helped me reason about the architecture was simple:

SQLite stores an incident record. Hindsight stores operational experience.

Recalling previous incidents with Hindsight

I integrated Hindsight as the persistent memory layer. When a new incident arrives, the backend creates a memory query containing the current service, status code, and error message.

The recall logic is intentionally small:

response = await client.arecall(
    bank_id=HINDSIGHT_BANK_ID,
    query=query,
    max_tokens=1000,
)

return [result.text for result in response.results[:3]]

The query asks Hindsight to find previous resolved production incidents that may help diagnose the current one. What matters to me here is that the new incident does not need to be an exact text match.

For example, one incident might say:

PostgreSQL connection pool exhaustion caused payment requests to fail.

A later incident might simply say:

Payment processing is failing because database connections cannot be acquired.

The wording is different, but the operational problem is similar. That is exactly the kind of situation where memory becomes more useful than searching for an exact string.

The Hindsight documentation was helpful while I was implementing the retain/recall flow and deciding what information should become long-term memory.

The moment the memory became useful

One of my test incidents involved the payment-api. The service was returning errors at /api/payment because it could not acquire PostgreSQL connections.

After investigation, I confirmed the root cause as PostgreSQL connection pool exhaustion. The successful resolution was to increase the connection pool from 20 to 50 and restart the payment-api service.

Later, I submitted another incident describing the same underlying problem differently. IncidentPilot did not start from zero. Hindsight recalled three relevant memories from previous incident experience.

That was the point where the project became more interesting to me. Saving history is easy. Actually retrieving useful experience when the wording changes is what makes the memory layer valuable.

From generic advice to memory-grounded recommendations

A large language model can already provide reasonable troubleshooting advice for a database error. Without memory, it might suggest:

Check database connectivity, inspect the connection pool, look for long-running queries, and verify server health.

There is nothing wrong with that answer. The problem is that it is generic. If my own system has already experienced the exact failure and successfully recovered from it, I want that history reflected in the recommendation.

So IncidentPilot sends both the current incident and the recalled Hindsight memories to the LLM. I tightened the recommendation prompt considerably during development:

STRICT RULES:
- Use only facts from the current incident and recalled memories.
- Never invent previous actions, incidents, metrics, deployments, or outcomes.
- If something is not supported by memory, say it should be verified.
- Maximum 3 recommended actions.

The response is also forced into a predictable structure:

  • Likely cause
  • Recommended actions
  • Memory evidence
  • Confidence

That constraint turned out to be important. An earlier version allowed much longer answers. It produced useful ideas, but it sometimes wandered into troubleshooting steps that were not clearly supported by the retrieved memory. For an incident-response system, I would rather have a short answer that clearly separates evidence from speculation.

The difference is easy to see.

Before memoryCheck the database configuration and connection limits.
After memoryA recent payment-api incident was caused by PostgreSQL connection pool exhaustion. Verify the current pool size; the previous successful fix increased it from 20 to 50 and restarted the service.

The second answer is useful for a different reason: it contains the system's own experience. That is the part of agent memory I find most compelling. The LLM does not suddenly know more general facts; it simply has better context from the system's history.

Learning only after a human confirms the fix

I did not want IncidentPilot to save every AI recommendation as permanent truth. That would be dangerous. An early diagnosis can be wrong, and storing a wrong diagnosis as successful operational knowledge could make later recommendations worse.

So the engineer closes the loop. After the incident is fixed, they provide:

  • the confirmed root cause,
  • the successful resolution,
  • and the resolution time.

Then IncidentPilot builds a memory containing the full incident context and retains it:

await client.aretain(
    bank_id=HINDSIGHT_BANK_ID,
    content=memory,
    context="Resolved IncidentPilot production incident",
)

The retained memory explicitly records that the resolution was confirmed successful. This creates the learning loop I wanted:

Incident → Recall → Recommend → Human resolves → Retain → Better context next time

A deployment problem taught me something useful too

One issue showed up only after deployment. Locally, IncidentPilot used SQLite without any trouble. But after deploying the FastAPI backend, I ran into a case where the frontend could analyze an incident but later received an "Incident not found" response when trying to save the resolution.

The problem was that I had coupled the memory-learning step too tightly to the temporary SQLite record.

I changed the flow so the resolution request can carry the important incident context itself. If the database record exists, the backend uses it. If it does not, the backend still has enough verified information to retain the resolved experience in Hindsight. That made the memory workflow much more resilient.

It also reinforced an architectural lesson: long-term agent knowledge should not depend on temporary application state surviving forever. For a production system, I would replace the current SQLite operational store with a durable PostgreSQL database.

What I learned

Building IncidentPilot changed how I think about agent systems in a few ways.

Memory quality matters more than memory quantity. During testing, repeated sample incidents created very similar memories. The recall still worked, but a production version needs better deduplication and memory hygiene.

Memory and generation should have separate jobs. Hindsight answers: what relevant experience has this system accumulated? The LLM answers: given the current incident and that experience, what should I investigate? Keeping those responsibilities separate makes the behavior much easier to understand.

Memory should be visible to the user. IncidentPilot explicitly shows how many memories were recalled and displays the evidence beside the recommendation. I prefer that to silently injecting memory into a prompt because the engineer can see why the agent is making a particular suggestion.

Keep a human in the loop before writing to long-term memory. In this use case, bad memory could be more harmful than no memory.

What I would build next

The next version of IncidentPilot would connect directly to operational systems. Monitoring or PagerDuty could create incidents automatically. Deployment history could help answer whether a failure started after a release. Slack or Microsoft Teams could become the interface where an engineer approves a remediation.

I would also add authentication, role-based access control, audit logging, a durable PostgreSQL incident store, and better memory deduplication.

But the basic idea would stay the same.

The most interesting part of this project was not getting an LLM to generate troubleshooting steps. LLMs can already do that. The interesting part was giving the system experience it could reuse.

Once one incident had been resolved and retained, the next similar failure no longer had to begin from zero.

And for incident response, that is exactly the kind of memory I wanted an agent to have.
